newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian newspapers blast Congress bid for power.
newsitem.headline: Indian newspapers blast Congress bid for power.

text.p: Indian newspapers on Monday blasted the Congress party's bid for power, calling it "sheer opportunism" and warning that the economy could not afford political turmoil.

The conservative daily The Hindu reacted to Congress chief Sitaram Kesri's Sunday decision to withdraw support to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's ten-month-old coalition government by running a rare editorial on its front page under its masthead.

"For the Congress...to suddenly choose this political moment to strike at the United Front government, just when some of its initiatives in key areas of policy appear to be acquiring some coherence and a sense of purpose, indicates a particular insensitivity to the national interest," The Hindu said.

The Business Standard said the turmoil would badly hurt business optimism and jeopardise Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's ambitious and market-friendly 1997/98 (April-March) budget, still awaiting parliamentary approval.

"Those, like Moody's (Investors Services) who had warned against continued political instability getting in the way of economic reform and therefore growth, now stand vindicated," the Business Standard said.

The Indian Express, in a front-page editorial titled "Demeaning Democracy", wrote: "The time and the manner in which it has been done, with a landmark budget awaiting parliamentary approval and the Pakistan foreign secretary in the capital, is shocking."
The Congress move occurred on the third day of crucial talks between senior Indian and Pakistani diplomats aimed at repairing frayed ties between the neighbours and bitter foes.
The talks, which were being held after a three-year gap, were scheduled to end on Monday, but as the Hindu noted, "have suddenly been emptied of political significance".

The same newspaper noted that Deve Gowda's coalition, despite differences among its 15 members, had granted "as never before in the last few decades" more autonomy to government ministries and added: "The United Front government had been able to take some major steps forward" on the economy and foreign policy.
The Asian Age said Kesri was gambling on crafting a new coalition that would continue to keep at bay the rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party, the biggest single party in parliament.

The BJP formed a short-lived government in May 1996 after Congress was defeated in inconclusive national elections. The BJP was unable to gather enough support to win a confidence vote, and was succeeded by the Deve Gowda coalition.
"Mr Kesri had personal motives too: the Congress was slipping away from his grasp, and there were growing fears that he would not survive as leader," the Asian Age said.
